questions.problem:
If $B$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $\lambda =4$ is an eigenvalue of $B,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $(B-4I)x=0$ has a nonzero solution

II. $\text{rank}(B-4I)=4$

III. $\text{nullity}(B-4I)\ne 0$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a $4\times 4$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=4=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Let's now apply the theorem to the matrix $M=B-4I.$

- Statement I is true. Notice that if $\lambda =4$ is an eigenvalue of $B,$ then the nonzero solutions of $(B-4I)x=0$ are eigenvectors of $B.$ As a result, the matrix $M=B-4I$ must be singular.

- Statement II is false. Since $M=B-4I$ is singular, by the invertible matrix theorem, we obtain that

$$
\text{rank}(B-4I)\ne 4.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $M=B-4I$ is singular, by the invertible matrix theorem, we obtain that

$$
\text{nullity}(B-4I)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
If $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $\text{rank}(A-3I)=4,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $\text{nullity}(A-3I)=0$

II. $A-3I$ is invertible

III. $\lambda =3$ is an eigenvalue of $A$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a $4\times 4$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=4=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $M$ has $4$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(M)+\text{nullity}(M)=4.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. According to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A-3I) & =4-\text{rank}(A-3I) \\  & =4-4 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statements II is true. By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A-3I)=0,$ we obtain that $A-3I$ must be invertible.

- Statement III is false. Notice that if $M=A-3I$ is invertible, then $(A-3I)x=0$ has only zero solution. As a result, $\lambda =3$ can not be an eigenvalue of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

II. $\text{nullity}(A-7I)=0$

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{2} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=2=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A-7I) & =2-\text{rank}(A-7I) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Notice that if $M=A-7I$ is singular, then $(A-7I)x=0$ has nonzero solutions which will be eigenvectors of $A.$ As a result, $\lambda =7$ is an eigenvalue of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
